In mathematics, in particular in [[measure theory]], there are different notions of  '''distribution function''' which are used in different context. Distribution functions (in the sense of measure theory) are a generalization of [[Cumulative distribution function|distribution functions (in the sense of probability theory)]].

== Definitions ==

The first definition<ref name="RudinRCA" /> presented here is typically used in Analysis ([[harmonic analysis]], [[Fourier Analysis]], and integration theory in general) to analysis properties of functions.

{{block indent | em = 1.5 | text = '''Definition 1:''' Suppose <math>(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)</math> is a [[measure space]], and let <math>f</math> be a real-valued [[measurable function]]. The distribution function associated with <math>f</math> is the function <math>d_f:[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}</math> given by<math display="block"> d_f(s)=\mu\Big(\{x\in X: |f(x)|>s\}\Big)</math>It is convenient also to define <math>d_f(\infty)=0</math>.}}

The function <math>d_f</math>  provides information about  the '''size''' of a measurable function <math>f</math>.

The next definitions of '''distribution function''' are straight generalizations of the notion of  [[Cumulative distribution function|distribution functions (in the sense of probability theory)]].

{{block indent | em = 1.5 | text = '''Definition 2.''' Let <math>\mu</math> be a finite [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] on the space <math>(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}),\mu)</math> of [[real number]]s, equipped with the [[Borel set|Borel <math>\sigma</math>-algebra]]. The   '''distribution function''' associated to <math>\mu</math> is the function <math> F_\mu \colon \R \to \R  </math> defined by <math display="block"> F_\mu(t)=\mu\big((-\infty,t]\big)</math>}}

It is well known result in measure theory<ref name="FollandRA" /> that if <math>F:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}</math> is a nondecreasing right continuous  function, then the function <math>\mu</math> defined on the collection of finite intervals of the form <math>(a,b]</math> by
<math display="block"> \mu\big((a,b]\big)=F(b)-F(a)</math>
extends uniquely to a measure <math>\mu_F</math> on a <math>\sigma</math>-algebra <math>\mathcal{M}</math> that included the Borel sets. Furthermore, if two such functions <math>F</math> and <math>G</math> induce the same measure, i.e. <math>\mu_F = \mu_G</math>, then <math>F-G</math> is constant. Conversely, if <math>\mu</math> is a measure on Borel subsets of the real line that is finite on compact sets,  then the function <math>F_\mu:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}</math> defined by
<math display="block"> F_\mu(t)= \begin{cases} \mu((0,t]) & \text{if } t\geq 0 \\ -\mu((t,0]) & \text{if } t < 0\end{cases}</math>
is a nondecreasing right-continuous function with <math>F(0)=0</math> such that <math>\mu_{F_\mu}=\mu</math>.

This particular ''distribution function'' is well defined whether <math>\mu</math> is finite or infinite; for this reason,<ref name="Kallenberg164" /> a few authors also refer to <math>F_{\mu}</math> as a distribution function of the measure <math> \mu </math>. That is:

{{block indent | em = 1.5 | text = '''Definition 3:''' Given the measure space <math>(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}),\mu)</math>, if <math>\mu</math> is finite on compact sets, then the nondecreasing right-continuous function <math>F_\mu</math> with <math>F_\mu(0)=0</math> such that <math display="block">\mu\big((a,b]) = F_\mu(b)-F_\mu(a)</math> is called the ''canonical'' distribution function associated to <math>\mu</math>.}}

== Example ==
As the measure, choose the [[Lebesgue measure]] <math> \lambda </math>. Then by Definition of <math> \lambda </math>
<math display="block"> \lambda((0,t])=t-0=t \text{ and } -\lambda((t,0])=-(0-t)=t</math>
Therefore, the distribution function of the Lebesgue measure is
<math display="block"> F_\lambda(t)=t</math>
for all <math> t \in \R </math>.

== Comments ==
* The distribution function <math>d_f</math> of a real-valued measurable function <math>f</math> on a measure space <math>(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)</math> is a monotone nonincreasing function, and it is supported on <math>[0,\mu(X)]</math>. If <math>d_f(s_0)<\infty</math> for some <math>s_0\geq0</math>, then <math display="block">\lim_{s\to\infty} d_f(s) = 0.</math>
* When the underlying measure <math>\mu</math> on <math>(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))</math> is finite, the distribution function <math>F</math> in Definition 3 differs slightly from the standard definition of the [[Cumulative distribution function|distribution function <math>F_\mu</math> (in the sense of probability theory)]] as given by Definition 2 in that for the former,  <math>F(0)=0</math> while for the latter, <math display="block"> \lim_{t \to - \infty} F_\mu(t)=0 \text{ and } \lim_{t \to  \infty} F_\mu(t)=\mu(\mathbb{R}). </math>
* When the objects of interest are measures in <math>(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))</math>, Definition 3 is more useful for infinite measures. This is the case because <math>\mu((- \infty, t])=\infty </math> for all <math>t\in\mathbb{R}</math>, which renders the notion in Definition 2 useless.
